title: Thieves in Italy steal 30,000 wine bottles worth €5m, reports say
description: Thieves have stolen 30,000 bottles of wine collectively worth about €5m (£4.2m) from a prestigious Italian winery, Italian media reports.Marchesi Anti
body: Thieves have stolen 30,000 bottles of wine collectively worth about €5m (£4.2m) from a prestigious Italian winery, Italian media reports.Marchesi Antinori, one of Italy's biggest family-owned wineries, said the theft at its storage facility in Tuscany took place on Saturday as the company was preparing to ship a consignment to customers abroad.At least seven masked men are believed to have deactivated the alarms, disabled the cameras and used company forklifts to load two large trucks of the company's prized Tignanello, Solaia and Guado al Tasso Tuscan reds.Renzo Cotarella, the chief executive, told Corriere della Sera this was the largest theft of its kind in Italy."A theft of this scale and value has certainly never occurred in Italy," he said.He added that he was hopeful the authorities would be able to trace the stolen wine."Two trucks full of merchandise can't just disappear into thin air. The Tuscan roads are full of cameras; perhaps with a bit of luck we'll be able to recover at least some of the bottles stolen from us."He told the Financial Times: "These wines have a great value and I don't know how they can sell all this wine around the world without being seen."The company believes the selection of bottles, which usually sell for between €150 and €500 each, suggests the thieves were wine connoisseurs and had inside knowledge.The theft was only discovered on Monday morning as staff arrived on site. No arrests have been made.Marchesi Antinori was founded in 1385 and exports to 170 countries. It had a revenue of €263m (£223m) last year.There has been a spate of wine thefts in Italy this year, including two in the northern Piedmont region where hundreds of thousands of euros worth of bottles were reportedly taken.

schema.headline: Thieves in Italy steal 30,000 wine bottles worth €5m, reports say

title: Fort Hood survivor supports gunman's execution by firing squad but questions livestream
description: A former US Army sergeant who survived the mass shooting on Fort Hood has said that while he supports the execution of the gunman by firing squad, he
body: A former US Army sergeant who survived the mass shooting on Fort Hood has said that while he supports the execution of the gunman by firing squad, he is concerned about it being livestreamed.Alonzo Lunsford, who was shot seven times, told the BBC that the "method is befitting" for Nidal Hasan because other methods like lethal injection would be "doing him a favour".Hasan, a US Army psychiatrist, fatally shot 13 unarmed US soldiers in a medical building at Fort Hood, in Texas, in 2009. But while Lunsford agreed with the method of execution, he said it was "not something you should view for entertainment purposes".Speaking to Radio 4's Today programme on Friday, he said: "To show the whole thing without it being censored for the general public, for me personally, I don't agree with that, but it's not about my personal belief."US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth said the public will be able to view a livestream of the execution, saying it is important for people to see the consequences of this kind of crime. If it goes ahead, and legal experts told the BBC it might not ever happen, it would be the first public execution in the US in almost a century.Lunsford explained that while he is concerned about the "effect" and "message" a livestream would send to younger people, when it comes to the survivors, their families and the families of the victims, they "should be able to look at it"."I'm gonna be there [to watch in person] and before they pull the trigger, I want him to look at me in my eyes and I look at him in his eyes and I want him to know: 'Dude you failed, I'm still here,'" he said."I don't really have any sympathy for him as far as firing squad vs lethal injection, hanging or gas chamber, because he didn't have that same compassion when he did the deed on 5 November," the former sergeant explained. "I think the method is befitting for him because the lethal injection - that's doing him a favour. Gas chamber? Is doing him a favour."But Lunsford said that as a Christian, he has forgiven Hasan because "I cannot heal if I don't forgive him"."We're taught that with your last breath you can ask for forgiveness and I think that's what he [Hasan] should do," he added.Telling his account of what happened that day, he said Hasan got out of his chair and jumped onto a counter, before pulling out a weapon and discharging rounds.Lunford said he was looking for an exit via the back door, which was "two or three strides" away from him when he was first shot above his left eye and then "hit two more times in my back" as he crawled behind a desk."At that point I played dead," he said. When Hasan moved on, he grabbed a nearby wounded soldier and went outside, where Lunsford said Hasan came up behind them and shot him again.One memory he said that "bothers" him from the day was of a woman who told Hasan she was pregnant."We heard a gunshot and the last thing that girl was saying was: 'Oh my god, my baby, my baby.'"Lunsford said personnel don't carry weapons in medical facilities, and that Hasan "took the coward's way out" to attack them there."And then for him to say he is fighting for his cause? I've read the Quran, and everything that he said he was doing that was in the Quran is not supported by the Quran," he explained.Hasan's execution was announced by the Pentagon earlier this week, in what will be the first military execution in more than 60 years.Legal experts have told the BBC there are a number of hurdles around the livestreaming of this which could mean it is successfully challenged in court.Some politicians have been vocal in their opposition.Democratic Senator Chris Murphy told CNN it was "disgusting" while Republican Senator Thom Tillis said public executions were what "oppressive dictators" did."It should not be happening in America," he added in a post on X., external

schema.headline: Fort Hood survivor supports gunman's execution by firing squad but questions livestream

title: Starlink: Why Elon Musk is taking on Mukesh Ambani and Jio over satellite internet
description: Elon Musk has questioned whether billionaire Mukesh Ambani is the "real boss of India" as his satellite internet company Starlink struggles to secure
body: Elon Musk has questioned whether billionaire Mukesh Ambani is the "real boss of India" as his satellite internet company Starlink struggles to secure final approval to launch in the country.The remark came a day after Musk accused unnamed powerful business interests of trying to block Starlink's entry into India. He then singled out Ambani, whose Reliance conglomerate owns Jio, India's biggest mobile network operator.India has rejected Musk's allegations, saying its satellite communications rules are fair and non-discriminatory.Ambani and Reliance Group have not responded to Musk's remarks. The BBC has reached out to them for commentThe row comes as competition grows in India's satellite internet market, with Reliance Jio and Bharti Airtel also preparing to launch services.The rivalry is complicated by the fact that Starlink has also partnered with Ambani's Reliance Jio and Bharti Airtel. In March 2025, both companies signed agreements with SpaceX to distribute Starlink equipment and services in India, subject to government approval. The companies also said they could explore sharing network infrastructure. The BBC has also reached out to Bharti Airtel for comment. Musk first made the allegations on Wednesday, accusing "certain oligarchs" of maintaining a "monopolistic chokehold" on Indian consumers."You can guess who they are," he wrote on X, external, adding that blocking Starlink was "a crime against the people of India".On Thursday, India's Ministry of Communications responded, saying that three operators - Starlink, Eutelsat OneWeb and Jio Satellite Communications - were at broadly the same stage of the approval process, with all three awaiting security clearances and spectrum allocation before they can launch commercial services."The suggestion that the framework or its application is unfair or discriminatory is baseless and misconceived," the ministry said, without naming Musk directly.Musk continued to question the delay, saying Starlink was already licensed in more than 165 countries."Starlink is licensed in over 165 countries and has spent five years complying with every single law and requirement of the government of India, so why still no license? Is Ambani the real boss of India?" he wrote on X on Thursday.Starlink, owned by Musk's SpaceX, uses satellites in low Earth orbit to provide internet access, particularly in remote areas where mobile networks and broadband cables are difficult or expensive to install.The company has been trying to enter India since 2021 and has secured key licences. But it still needs final security clearances and spectrum allocation before it can begin commercial services.Wednesday's row unfolded as senior executives from Starlink, Reliance Jio and Bharti Airtel gathered at the India Mobile Congress in Delhi, where all three companies discussed their plans for satellite internet services.Speaking at the event, Akash Ambani, chairman of Reliance Jio Infocomm and Mukesh Ambani's son, said the company was developing its own satellite communications technology and working towards regulatory approvals.Asked by a reporter about Musk's allegations, Akash declined to comment and only said, "We want to be heads down and deliver value to our Indian consumers."    Bharti Airtel chairman Sunil Bharti Mittal said his company's satellite venture was also awaiting government approvals.SpaceX executive Lauren Dreyer, who oversees Starlink's business operations, said the company had spent years working with Indian regulators and had built security controls into its network to meet the country's requirements.Security has been a key concern surrounding Starlink's entry into India. In 2024, Indian authorities said they had recovered Starlink equipment during a drug-smuggling investigation in the remote Andaman and Nicobar Islands and an army operation in the northeastern state of Manipur.Musk said at that time that Starlink's service had never been active in India, arguing that the equipment recovered by authorities could not have been using its satellite network.Questions also remain over how affordable the service would be for Indian consumers, particularly those in rural areas.India is one of the world's largest internet markets but access remains uneven, particularly in remote areas where mobile networks and broadband cables are difficult or expensive to build.Musk has argued that Starlink could help bridge this gap. "Starlink in India would enable high-speed, affordable internet connectivity for those who can't afford current prices or who don't have a connection at all!" he wrote on X on Wednesday. The company has yet to announce prices for India, but some experts say its plans elsewhere suggest the service could be beyond the reach of many Indian households.In the US, Starlink's residential plans start at $55 a month, although prices and equipment costs vary by plan and location.

schema.headline: Starlink: Why Elon Musk is taking on Mukesh Ambani and Jio over satellite internet

title: Zack Polanski faces greatest crisis of his leadership so far
description: In the aftermath of a by-election, the focus is usually on the winner. Not this time.Make no mistake, the new MP for Holborn and St Pancras in north L
body: In the aftermath of a by-election, the focus is usually on the winner. Not this time.Make no mistake, the new MP for Holborn and St Pancras in north London, Sagal Abdi-Wali, has quite the story to tell.She arrived in the UK as a child refugee from Somalia in the 1990s, grew up locally in Camden, became a councillor four years ago, the council leader in May and is now Sir Keir Starmer's successor as the MP.But in the offices of Camden Council at three o'clock this morning, the focus of the press pack, me included, was on Zack Polanski, the leader of the Green Party of England and Wales, as we waited for the result.This constituency has long been a safe Labour seat – the political home of the former prime minister and before that the former cabinet minister Frank Dobson. So a Labour victory here falls in the column marked "relief" for Downing Street rather than "jubilation". Nonetheless, the Greens did very well in local elections in London in May, riding the crest of a political wave which began shortly after Polanski became the party's leader just over a year ago.His failure to win here will prompt questions from some about stalling momentum, but the party can and does point to the big swing to them since the general election and a result that was by a long way the second best ever result for them at a Westminster by-election.Incidentally, in finishing third the Conservatives have beaten Reform UK for the first time in an English by-election since the general election. It seems likely that Reform's result was hampered by Restore Britain, who managed almost half as many votes as Reform did, in a constituency not very favourable to either party.But the real reason for the nocturnal scramble of cameras, microphones and questions for Polanski had little to do with the by-election – and everything to do with a vote at the Green Party's conference in Brighton last weekend.Activists there passed a motion declaring Zionism as a form of racism.The motion defined Zionism as an ideology supporting "an ethnonationalist Jewish state" and backed a "single democratic Palestinian state in all of historic Palestine", which includes modern-day Israel.Polanski didn't take part in the vote because, he said, he chose to campaign in Holborn and St Pancras instead. And he repeatedly declined to do interviews, as the pressure on him as ratcheted up.But this morning he did speak to journalists.He told BBC Breakfast that if he had he been there for the vote he "would have voted for the amendments".Asked if he would have voted against the motion in the hall on that day, Polanski said: "the motion as amended I would have voted for, the motion unamended I wouldn't have voted for."He added:  "I think it's an imperfect motion, there's parts I disagree with and parts I agree with."Some in the party are furious about what has happened in recent days, with one figure telling me: "He has created a monster he either can't or won't control." Green Party membership has increased more than three fold in the last year and internal critics of Polanski say this includes hard-left campaigners focused on the Middle East rather than environmental concerns.Within the party and beyond it, a row is now boiling. Polanski, who is himself Jewish, has been banned from Israel. The Jewish Leadership Council and the Board of Deputies of British Jews have criticised the party, as have sister Green parties in Europe.And – significantly – the former party leader and one of the most important figures in the Green movement of her generation, Caroline Lucas, told BBC Newsnight Polanski had failed to show leadership over the issue. She also failed to back him carrying on as leader.Asked by reporters after the by-election result if he could continue as leader, Polanski insisted "of course I can carry on".He did not explicitly reject the motion his party has passed, saying there was an "ongoing genocide and the displacement of the Palestinian people". "I believe that is clearly racist," he added.Israel has repeatedly denied its actions in Gaza amount to genocide.And asked if he believed in a two-state solution – an Israeli and Palestinian state existing peacefully alongside each other – he said "I believe it is not our role to decide".He repeated that "it is my job to reassure people and make sure that we bring our party together". "No one will be excluded in the Green Party based on faith and religion," he said.But Polanski now confronts the greatest crisis of his leadership so far. He faces open, public insurrection about his judgement from senior figures internally and opprobrium from plenty of others beyond the party.The campaign in Holborn and St Pancras might be over. The questions for Polanski certainly aren't.

schema.headline: Zack Polanski faces greatest crisis of his leadership so far

title: Neha Bora: India's feisty Gen Z protester who is taking on Modi
description: When India's Gen Z-led protesters return to Delhi this weekend for demonstrations seeking the resignation of the country's top election official, one
body: When India's Gen Z-led protesters return to Delhi this weekend for demonstrations seeking the resignation of the country's top election official, one of the prominent faces at the forefront will be that of a 29-year-old PhD student.Neha Bora is a theatre artist and activist who has been with the All India Students' Association (Aisa), a Left-wing organisation known for campus politics, for the past decade and been its president for the past two years.But Neha's - who uses "they" and "them" as personal pronouns - visibility is no longer limited to campuses.Viral videos over the past few days show them being dragged through the street by a group of female police officials, climbing on top of police barricades, raising their fist and shouting slogans, and being detained.Photos of them smiling while being carried away by policewomen have also gone viral.In a recent BBC Bangla interview, external, Neha played down the attention they've been receiving."I know it happened in front of the camera so it seems like it's something different," they said. "But I have seen all student activists with the Left doing the same things that I have been doing. It's just that there is a camera on me, so people think something different is happening."The attention on Neha comes at a time when several high-profile protests are being held on India's streets in what is being seen as one of the biggest challenges to Prime Minister Narendra Modi's 12 years in power.There's the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) - a Gen Z-led online satirical movement - that held weeks-long protests in Delhi in the summer over education reforms. It ended in July only after education minister Dharmendra Pradhan's resignation.Separately, some of India's opposition parties, especially the Congress, have also taken to the streets over electoral reforms. For the past few days, videos of Congress leaders Rahul Gandhi and Priyanka Gandhi Vadra being shoved and jostled and detained have gone viral and made headlines in India.Saturday's protest in Delhi has been called by the CJP, which is seeking the resignation of India's Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar over allegations of manipulating electoral rolls to favour Modi's BJP. Both the Election Commission and the BJP have rejected the accusation.Although not a member of the CJP, Neha has said their group would also participate. Born in the northern state of Uttarakhand, Neha lived in different cities as a child as their army officer father moved for his postings. After graduating from Delhi University, they did a master's degree from Ambedkar University in the capital and are now a PhD student at the prestigious Jawaharlal Nehru University (JNU).Neha first came into the spotlight in the summer during the CJP's protest over education reforms.Neha and Aisa were at the protest from the start, but not many knew them at that point. That changed after 28 June, when educationist and scientist Sonam Wangchuk began a hunger strike in CJP's support and Neha and a few others from Aisa also joined him."It was an obvious choice for us. We've been protesting against paper leaks and education reforms for a long time," Neha later said in an interview.While most of the attention was focused on Wangchuk, whose reputation and presence galvanised the movement, Neha's outspokenness and combative speeches began to get them noticed.After Wangchuk and others were moved to hospital, Neha continued fasting despite having lost 8kg. Even after being moved to hospital, they said in a video: "The fight continues. Once I've recovered, we'll meet you again on the streets to continue our fight for our right."After the protests ended in July, Neha has established themselves as a Gen Z leader who's courted by the CJP and media, besides appearing alongside Rahul Gandhi at press conferences.But Neha's involvement with Aisa and leftist politics and statements criticising PM Modi, Home Minister Amit Shah and other BJP leaders have also led to "lots of disagreements with my family as my parents are staunch supporters of BJP".And last month, at least three police complaints were lodged, external in Uttar Pradesh state by BJP against Neha for making "objectionable remarks" against the chief minister - they came two days after Aisa's police complaint that Neha had received death threats, external.Neha, who has been travelling to many Indian cities to participate in protests in support of students, also made headlines when a man allegedly threw ink, external at them during a protest march in Jharkhand state. A photo Neha shared on Instagram showed their face streaked with ink stains. Police said they had detained the man. The noisy protests and repeated detentions have earned Neha a reputation for being a street fighter."The streets have always dictated the course of politics in this country and they will continue to do so, more so in the coming few years," they told BBC Bangla."If we look at the social changes of the recent past, those social changes did not come from people sitting in parliament; they came from the streets," they said.Now as the authorities gear up for 10 October's protest at Jantar Mantar against CEC Kumar, Neha and Aisa have said they would be back in the streets with the CJP  to "protect democracy".

schema.headline: Neha Bora: India's feisty Gen Z protester who is taking on Modi

title: Cyberpunk 2077 movie adaptation from Paramount on the way
description: A live-action movie version of smash hit video game Cyberpunk 2077 is being developed by Paramount Pictures.The Hollywood studio is working with produ
body: A live-action movie version of smash hit video game Cyberpunk 2077 is being developed by Paramount Pictures.The Hollywood studio is working with producer Lorenzo di Bonaventura, known for his work on the Transformers films, and CD Projekt Red (CDPR), the developer of the sci-fi role-playing game.CDPR's joint-chief executive Michał Nowakowski said in a statement, external the company was "excited about Paramount as a future partner who shares our creative ambitions for the Cyberpunk franchise".Details of the film's story, potential release date and casting information are yet to be revealed.Despite a troubled launch in 2020, the Cyberpunk 2077 video game, which stars Keanu Reeves, has sold more than 40 million copies worldwide.The John Wick star plays rockstar Johnny Silverhand, a terrorist whose consciousness is stored on a chip inside the body of main character V.Set in Night City, a fictional metropolis in a dystopian version of California, players work to uncover a conspiracy involving the shady Arasaka megacorporation.An expansion, Phantom Liberty, starring Idris Elba was released in 2023 and has sold more than 15 million copies, according to CDPR.Cyberpunk has already been successfully adapted into a popular animated series - Edgerunners - with a second season due to premiere on Netflix later this month.The streamer also produced The Witcher, an adaptation of CDPR's massively popular fantasy role-playing series.It originally starred former Superman actor Henry Cavill, but he was replaced by Liam Hemsworth in the show's fourth season.

schema.headline: Cyberpunk 2077 movie adaptation from Paramount on the way

title: Russian strikes and approaching winter force some in Kyiv to pack bags and flee
description: Figure caption, Watch: Olena explains what she cannot live near in order to stay safeByPaul AdamsDiplomatic correspondent, in KyivAs Russia's attacks
body: Figure caption, Watch: Olena explains what she cannot live near in order to stay safeByPaul AdamsDiplomatic correspondent, in KyivAs Russia's attacks on Ukraine's cities intensify and autumn's cooler temperatures hint at another tough winter to come, Ukrainians are wrestling with how to meet the twin challenges ahead: Russian drone and missile strikes and the biting cold."It was a very difficult winter last year in Kyiv," says mother of two Mariia Shostak, who is now packing her bags and leaving her small flat.With prolonged periods of sub-zero temperatures and frequent power cuts brought about by Russia's attack on the country's power grid, last winter was one of the hardest so far."There were some days and weeks that were unbearable. I started thinking I'm not going through another winter like this."Mariia is not even waiting for winter. Russia's latest assaults on the capital have forced her hand."Everything changed in late August and the beginning of September, when Kyiv started being attacked around the clock," she said."Earlier, the drones and missiles were intercepted somewhere on the outskirts. Now it was happening in the centre, right above our heads."Image caption, Wreckage from Russian drones can be found on the streets of the capitalAfter weeks of escalating Russian attacks, which by the end of September had included petrol stations, power plants and key bridges over the Dnipro river, Kyiv mayor Vitaly Klitschko said the city was facing a "very dramatic situation".The attacks, he said, were "tearing Kyiv apart".Mariia's children, four-year-old Artur and Kira, who's two, were both born after Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022.Unwilling to subject them to another miserable, dangerous winter, she's taking them abroad. They plan to spend the winter in Hurghada, on Egypt's Red Sea coast. It's cheaper than Europe, Mariia explains, and warmer too."I don't feel safe in Ukraine in any way," she says.Polls show that many Ukrainians are feeling the same way, even if not everyone has yet made such a radical decision.A September survey by the Gradus research company found that 40% of Ukrainians were considering relocating if living conditions continued to deteriorate; 35% said they would not move elsewhere, while 25% were undecided."People are thinking about a combination of stress factors," Evgeniya Blyznyuk, Gradus's founder and CEO, told us. "Not just about electricity and blackouts like last winter. Russians are targeting big logistics centres, which means that the population is worrying about products, about food during the winter."Image caption, Iryna's young daughter Polina is struggling to cope and suffers from anxietyRussia's recent attacks on Kyiv's bridges, petrol stations and schools have increased the sense of danger and foreboding.For families with young children, the situation feels especially urgent.Last winter, Iryna, who asked us not to use her surname, says her three-year-old daughter Polina found it hard to cope."Sometimes we didn't have heating for weeks and the temperature inside the apartment was zero or five degrees," she tells us. "So being here with a little child that is sick all the time was not OK."The family's recent experiences have only compounded Polina's difficulties."We had two missile attacks this year," Iryna says.Image source, SuppliedImage caption, Iryna and Polina's home is in this apartment block on the edge of the capitalThe first explosion, in early June, blew out several windows in the family's home on the north-western edge of Kyiv. A month later, after some of the damage had been repaired, a second blast, close to the foot of their 10-storey apartment block, propelled a wave of earth into the flat, forcing the family to move into temporary accommodation.Polina's health has deteriorated. She suffers from extreme anxiety, which has brought on bouts of incontinence, vomiting and uncontrollable shaking."Now we have this neurological problem with her so that's the reason we're thinking about leaving," Iryna says. "There are new symptoms after each shelling."Iryna, whose husband is in the army, has not yet decided where to go. Her work with an international NGO may allow her to work remotely from Poland."Our president says that it is better to leave Kyiv because this is target number one," she says.For other Kyiv residents, the solution lies closer to home: in the vast open spaces of Ukraine's countryside.Image caption, Olena Konoplia says she is already sleeping better since her move to a more remote locationOlena Konoplia tells us she spent weeks looking for a suitable location before settling on a cottage in a rural community two hours outside the capital."I decided the better option will be a little village without any factories, any [warehouses] and any railway stations," Olena explains."Everything that can be a Russian target."On the day we visited, Olena was busy ferrying supplies to the house and supervising the installation of a new door.In keeping with Ukrainian tradition, a priest has already been around to bless her new home.The cottage has gas-powered convection heaters, but in an adjacent barn a stack of firewood will help to keep Olena warm in the event of power cuts. She has already installed high-speed internet, necessary for her work at a Kyiv-based charitable foundation.At a time when air raid sirens sound constantly in Kyiv and explosions can be heard almost every day, the peace and quiet of the village is what Olena says she needs most."After several nights here, when I can sleep, just sleep, without any explosions, without any sirens, I feel better," she says. "I can work, write my articles, I feel good."Olena's elderly mother will soon be joining her."She lives in a pretty dangerous district in Kyiv and it's harmful for her health," she explains.Of course, not everyone can afford a cottage in the countryside or a months-long trip abroad.Most Kyiv residents will do what they can to survive another tough winter in the capital, just as they have before.Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, Supermarkets in Kyiv have been experiencing shortages of goods at timesThe authorities are taking steps to prepare. Some of Kyiv's most vulnerable citizens – the elderly and women with young children – are being offered places in converted sanatoriums and rehabilitation centres in the city's forested outskirts.Meanwhile, a network of around 15 small-scale power plants has been constructed around the city over the past 18 months in an effort to shore up Kyiv's battered power grid.The plants, constructed in fortified bunkers and protected from drone attack by huge steel cages, are each capable of providing electricity and heat to several hundred of the city's high-rise apartment blocks.But with energy companies already talking about scheduled power cuts and supermarkets experiencing periodic shortages of some goods, the pressures to leave are growing.Evgeniya Blyznyuk says she does not expect to see a mass exodus from the capital and says most people have yet to make up their minds, reluctant to jeopardise their jobs or take children out of school."They will postpone it until conditions become really unliveable," she says.Additional reporting by Mariana Matveichuk and Anastasiia Levchenko.

schema.headline: Russian strikes and approaching winter force some in Kyiv to pack bags and flee

title: How soon into dating should you reveal your salary?
description: I've been with my boyfriend for two years and don't know his salaryFigure caption, Watch: How soon into dating do you talk about your salary? We ask N
body: I've been with my boyfriend for two years and don't know his salaryFigure caption, Watch: How soon into dating do you talk about your salary? We ask New Yorkers and LondonersByYasmin RufoBusiness reporter Reporting fromNew YorkUpdated 1 hour agoYou know their favourite restaurant, what happened with their ex and their most embarrassing childhood story. But do you know how much your partner earns?Money remains one of dating's trickier conversations. Bring it up too early and it can sound like you're sizing up their bank balance. But leave it too long and you could be planning a future with someone without knowing much about their finances at all.We spoke to 20-somethings in New York City to see if there was a sweet spot for when to talk salaries.Image caption, Willa says she doesn't know what her partner earns even though he knows her salary Willa Morton, 25, says she doesn't think couples necessarily need to reveal their salaries at all."It's just a number and you can gauge how much someone makes based on the way they live and how much they spend," she says.Willa, who works in tech sales, has talked to her boyfriend about not earning very much herself but hasn't asked him for a figure in return.He's a company founder and, though his income varies, she knows that he earns more than she does."He's more free-spending whereas I'm always saying, 'That's too expensive, that costs too much, we don't need to spend that.'"Their dates typically cost around $200 (£150) and he usually pays, while she picks up smaller bills such as coffees."It's an unspoken rule that he will pick up the bigger bills."Image caption, Vik says if someone brought up salary and spending on a first date they probably wouldn't be the right person for himFor many, there's a fairly clear dividing line as to when you talk about salary, spending habits and debt and that's when you become an official couple.Alexa Ludato, 25, who works in insurance, says she'd only have the conversation when she was official with someone.Before then, she would "like to have an idea of what their job is, but not how much they make".Her friend, Vik Sunderaj, 22, agrees. "You should only discuss it once you get into a serious relationship."He thinks a salary question on the first few dates is "a little crazy"."If they asked, I would be honest, but I wouldn't bring it up," he says. And if his date really wanted to know his salary, "it probably means they wouldn't be the right person for me".'Asking my salary is a red flag'Others feel even more strongly about being asked too soon. Twenty-six-year-old Bridget Shurdut, who works in sales, says she would find it "incredibly odd" if someone asked about her salary within the first few dates."I don't think I'd continue to see that person. I'd answer the question, but it would be a red flag for me."For her, someone's current salary isn't necessarily particularly useful information anyway as she says she's much more interested in "whether someone is ambitious and driven than what they earn monetarily".Dating and relationship coach Kate Mansfield, says money conversations "should start much earlier than many people think". "In the first few dates you should talk about how each of you approaches spending, saving, generosity, lifestyle and financial independence as these things shape compatibility." Image caption, Emily's been in a relationship for two years and has not discussed salaries yetBecoming official doesn't necessarily mean swapping payslips though.Insurance worker Emily Moretta, 26, has been with her boyfriend for two years and says they still haven't explicitly told each other their salaries and "he doesn't know how much I make".She assumes he probably has a rough idea, but says neither has ever felt the need to ask."Maybe down the line we would, when it gets more serious," she says, adding that they would have to be at the stage of moving in together before talking about it.

schema.headline: How soon into dating should you reveal your salary?

title: 'Careless use of AI is the real threat - not the ghost stories'
description: Image source, Alvaro Alvarez/ BBCImage caption, Meredith Whittaker believes science doesn't support the idea that AI will turn against humansByMegha M
body: Image source, Alvaro Alvarez/ BBCImage caption, Meredith Whittaker believes science doesn't support the idea that AI will turn against humansByMegha MohanGender and identity correspondentWarning: This article contains strong language.Meredith Whittaker has little patience for the AI doom that dominates headlines - she thinks warnings of AI turning on humanity is a fear "not anchored in science"."The risk is very real," says the boss of the Signal Foundation, which runs the encrypted messaging app of the same name, "but it's not the shiny ghost stories the wild-eyed boys are talking about".Instead, she believes the more immediate danger is the technology being used carelessly. She cites an alleged incident, reported by CNN, in which a chatbot used by US intelligence invented information about a Chinese vessel carrying nuclear material, reportedly leading the US to prepare a military response."We almost went to war with China," she tells BBC Global Women."A system that produces faulty intelligence and almost gets us into a war with China should not be considered super-intelligent by any standards."Signal has an estimated 40-70 million users - a drop in the ocean next to WhatsApp, which has billions.But it is renowned for its tough stance on protecting users' privacy - it hides who is sending a message from its own servers, limiting the data available to outside observers or hackers.Project Maven protestTime magazine named Whittaker one of the most powerful people in AI. She moves through the rooms where its future is discussed, from Silicon Valley boardrooms to Downing Street, Davos and the Vatican.She studied literature at university and joined Google in 2006 as an entry-level temp with no computer science degree.In late 2017, she made her name when a colleague told her about Project Maven, a secret Google contract with the US Department of Defense to build AI for drone targeting.She understood what it meant to "compress the kill chain": to shrink the time between a machine flagging a target and someone deciding to fire, reducing deliberation. With thousands of colleagues, she pushed back."This is going to launder bad intelligence and bad data," she remembers arguing publicly.The following year Whittaker helped organise a walkout, in which some 20,000 staff protested against the company's handling of several issues, including what they felt was the rushed introduction of new technology. Google dropped the contract and Palantir picked it up.Image source, Alvaro Alvarez/ BBCImage caption, Whittaker criticises venture capitalists' lack of support for startups led by womenShe draws a direct line from Maven to the US missile attack on a school in Iran this year, which she says relied on the system and on outdated intelligence that identified the school as a military target."This is exactly what we were warning about in 2017," she says.In response, Palantir told Global Women there was "no evidence that Palantir's software was at fault in this terrible tragedy". It added that "Palantir is not responsible for the underlying data nor identifying intelligence deficiencies". And earlier this year it's UK and Europe boss, Louis Mosley told the BBC that "there's always a human in the loop, so there is always a human that makes the ultimate decision". The US military has yet to release the findings of its investigation into the Minab strike, but Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has said it would "never target civilian targets".'I have a backbone'Governments, including the UK's, argue for more access to conversations on messaging apps. They say this is to protect women and children.At London Tech Week 2026, then Prime Minister Keir Starmer said technology companies would be expected to detect and block nude images on children's devices, or face legislation. Whittaker argues children would be able to circumvent any such measures, calling the government's approach "an unprecedented regime of communication and information controls".The Department for Science, Innovation and Technology told the BBC it is preparing legislation.Would Signal leave any country, the UK included, that forced it to weaken its encryption?"Yes! My God, I have a backbone," she says. "It doesn't change based on mood. It doesn't change based on consultants."Faced with exposing people "who rely on us, sometimes in the context of life or death, to surveillance that could be weaponised against them", she says, "we would leave the market".The app is fully or partially blocked in Russia, China and Iran.Image source, Alvaro Alvarez/ BBCImage caption, Whittaker advises women in tech to stand up to bulliesRani Govender, Head of Child Safety Online at the National Society for Prevention of Cruelty to Children, told the BBC it hears from children who have been groomed and moved on to end-to-end encrypted platforms, where they are coerced into creating child sexual abuse material."Tech companies are responsible for the design choices they make, and they cannot ignore the risks those choices can create for children."But Signal does have support from some women's groups, often those from the Global South who use the app themselves."In a time of state surveillance and cyber-attacks, Signal is a tool for survival," says Hera Hussain, founder of the gender abuse charity Chayn, which is active throughout South Asia. "With any platform, it can be used by bad actors too, and we have to hold that truth too."'What do we do about the kitchens?'I put to Whittaker a case from Canada, where police officers shared racist and misogynistic messages in a Signal group which leaked only when one of them passed it on to the media. A lawyer for one officer said the men believed Signal was as private and safe as their own home."If they had that conversation in the kitchen and their bro snitched, would it be: 'What are we doing about kitchens?'" she asks. "It has to work for everyone or it works for no-one. This is the principle of fundamental rights. They apply even to assholes."She points to a US woman jailed after Meta handed over messages showing she helped her daughter access abortion in a state where it had been criminalised. Private communication, she says, protects people from many kinds of harm - "an abusive spouse, a misogynist law enforcement officer with access to a database, or an authoritarian government that doesn't think women should get educated".What would she want to say to a woman who wants to enter the tech field but is intimidated by the gendered aspect of the profession?"Do you love it?" she says."Do you sit down at a terminal and feel a rush of energy? Do you enjoy playing with and defining AI systems?"Then she pauses and says: "Are you able to navigate interesting and gnarly environments where not everyone is going to be chill? Because there's nothing more dangerous than being a coward in front of a bully."I ask her if these environments are full of bullies.Her colleague says, "I think that's 2pm" - the time we agreed to end the interview.Meredith smiles. "I'd say don't be a simp," she says, using a term for someone who shows extreme deference to authority figures. "It's not going to help you. Don't laugh at the joke if you don't think it's funny."Additional reporting by Katie RobertsThis is part of the Global Women series from the BBC World Service, sharing untold and important stories from around the globe

schema.headline: 'Careless use of AI is the real threat - not the ghost stories'

title: Man jailed for attempted murder after stabbing ex in Carmarthen Park
description: McKenna had waited for Sidaway to enter the park on 29 January with her dog, before crouching down in the bushes, ready to launch his attack.A jury at
body: McKenna had waited for Sidaway to enter the park on 29 January with her dog, before crouching down in the bushes, ready to launch his attack.A jury at Swansea Crown Court heard McKenna was "angry" after their relationship ended a few months earlier, and it was "luck" that she did not die, with her winter coat helping to save her.During the trial, he told the jury he had put the newest, sharpest knife from his kitchen in his bag that morning, with the intention of using it to hurt Sidaway.He said he wanted to cause Sidaway "serious harm" but not kill her."I felt she was reluctant to re-engage with me, and not even say hello," he said. As she approached, he stabbed her multiple times, in what he agreed was "a rage of anger".He told the court he was "shocked" at what he had done."I was aiming for her shoulder area and the upper body. I didn't want to kill her."He said the attack was interrupted after Sidaway told him to stop and screamed,  and a neighbour shouted.Neighbour Susan Edwards told the court during the trial in July she heard "high-pitched screaming" and the "bushes shaking" before a man ran away.Sidaway phoned for an ambulance and said: "I've been stabbed by my ex-partner... he's been stalking me".McKenna fled the scene following the attack, and said he dumped his rucksack, with the knife, at an allotment near the park after he ate a yoghurt there.He then walked to Bronwydd, a village about three miles (4km) north of Carmarthen, along the River Gwili."I found some shelter, a quiet woodland away from the road," he said."I was devastated and kept having flashbacks."He said he was there for three nights, before he travelled via taxi and bus to Bronglais Hospital in Aberystwyth, Ceredigion.Police bodycam footage was shown to the jury of Sidaway sitting on her doorstep with paramedics, covered in blood.The jury heard there were 17 areas of damage to Sidaway's coat, and were shown images of her "extensively blood-stained" clothing as well as injuries to her chest, arm and hand. Sidaway did not wish to share a victim personal statement.Sentencing McKenna, Thomas said: "You had been in a relationship with a woman of whose vulnerabilities you would have been fully aware."When she decided, as was entirely her prerogative, that she no longer wanted to be in a relationship with you, you reacted, as you had done in the past, immaturely, and more significantly with violence."You stalked her in the park in Carmarthen that morning, then you returned in the afternoon with exactly the same intention. It was planned, and it was wholly calculated."You stabbed her no fewer than 11 times. Three of those being to the chest and therefore heart area."That lady only survived because it was a cold day and she as wearing five layers under a thick coat. But after you did that, you left her to die in bushes in a park."You only handed yourself in when you developed frostbite from sleeping rough."He said McKenna was "full of self-pity".The court heard McKenna had been convicted of assault against an ex-partner in August 2016, after pushing her neck and pulling her hair.Prosecution barrister James Wilson said it demonstrated that he was "unwilling to accept the end of that relationship".Caroline Rees KC, defending, said the "best point in mitigation" she could make on his behalf was that of the "remorse" he had shown since the incident.She referenced a letter from defendant in which he "expresses his sorrow and regret" for what happened, she said.Lucy Mansfield, of the Crown Prosecution Service said: "McKenna's actions were cold and calculated, deliberately taking a knife to a public place to attack his ex-partner."He committed a shocking act of violence, which must have been terrifying for the victim."We will continue to work with our partners in the criminal justice system to tackle these abhorrent offences."Welsh Women's Aid Chief Executive Sara Kirkpatrick said this was a "carefully planned" attack."Sadly, post-separation abuse, stalking, following a domestically abusive relationship is remarkably common," she said."While we can ask ourselves how we make our spaces and places safer, this was an intentional act by an individual who made a plan and chose a place, and identified where his victim would be.She added that was why the charity campaigned for social change, "so that we don't find ourselves in a place where individuals think that pursuing vengeance in this manner is an acceptable route".Swansea Crown Court heard he will spend two thirds of his sentence in prison, before being released on licence.

schema.headline: Man jailed for attempted murder after stabbing ex in Carmarthen Park

title: Everton owners The Friedkin Group consider selling club
description: Everton owners The Friedkin Group (TFG) are exploring the sale of the club less than two years after taking control.The American group completed a tak
body: Everton owners The Friedkin Group (TFG) are exploring the sale of the club less than two years after taking control.The American group completed a takeover of the club in 2024 in a deal believed to be worth in excess of £400m.In a statement, TFG said after prioritising stability, investment and the opening of Everton's new stadium last year, the time is right "to consider the next chapter"."The Friedkin Group is exploring new investment options for Everton Football Club, including the potential sale of a controlling interest," TFG said."When TFG became custodians of Everton, the club faced significant financial uncertainty and challenges both on and off the pitch. The immediate priority was to provide the stability, investment and support needed to secure the club's future, including helping to bring the long-promised stadium to completion for its deserving supporters."With that foundation now safely in place, the time is right to consider the next chapter for Everton."TFG, led by chairman Dan Friedkin, outlined a vision for a "sustainable and successful" future for the club when they took over, but its leadership came under scrutiny during the summer transfer window.In September, David Moyes said he had never met or spoken to Friedkin, who is based in Houston, since returning as manager in January 2025.Friedkin leaves the day-to-day running of the club to his son-in-law Rishi Majithia, who works in tandem with chief executive Angus Kinnear.Fans reacted angrily when news broke that Everton had accepted a £40m bid from Nottingham Forest for one of their prized assets, England Under-19 midfielder Harrison Armstrong.Everton eventually pulled out of the deal, but supporters remained frustrated by the selling of Beto to Fiorentina shortly after.The move left the Toffees with just one recognisable striker in 23-year-old Frenchman Thierno Barry.TFG added that they will only "entertain interest from parties who we strongly believe will be the right stewards to take the club forward"."Throughout this process, TFG's focus will remain unchanged. We will support the club in all ways necessary to achieve success on the pitch and will continue efforts to make a positive difference in the communities the club serves," the statement continued.The decision of Everton's owners TFG to explore selling the club comes as no great surprise after the turbulent events of recent times.A fracture opened up between TFG and Everton's fanbase over the controversial attempt to sell highly-rated teenager Armstrong late in the transfer window, before a botched deadline day left manager Moyes with only 18 senior outfield players.The failed sale of Armstrong, as well as the departure of Iliman Ndiaye to Manchester City for £65m, was bolted on to a cautious approach to the markets that suggested limited ambition on the part of TFG.It was in sharp contrast to the more hands-on approach at AS Roma, the other club owned by TFG, who bring in the additional riches of playing in the Champions League.Moyes revealing he had never spoken to Friedkin, who has not attended an Everton game since the Scot was reappointed as manager 21 months ago, strengthened the belief among supporters that TFG were effectively absentee owners.TFG secured a deal for 99.5% of the club, succeeding former owner Farhad Moshiri in 2024 after Everton had fallen into financial crisis.Since then, TFG have put the club on a stable financial footing and Everton have moved into a new stadium - although this was effectively done before their takeover - and have made the club an attractive proposition to potential buyers.This will be TFG's main achievement in what will, when Everton is sold, be regarded as an unspectacular tenure.

schema.headline: Everton owners The Friedkin Group consider selling club

title: Celebrity Traitors episode three: Emotions run high as two players banished
description: Emotions run high at the round table as Celebrity Traitors banish two playersImage caption, Actress Sharon Rooney was visibly shocked to find which pl
body: Emotions run high at the round table as Celebrity Traitors banish two playersImage caption, Actress Sharon Rooney was visibly shocked to find which players returned to breakfast during Thursday's episodeBySteven McIntoshEntertainment reporterSpoiler warning: This article reveals details from the third episode of The Celebrity Traitors, series two.We normally expect raised voices, conflicting theories and a dramatic showdown from the Celebrity Traitors. But as this year's first round table got under way, the writing was on the castle wall.Viewers who often get frustrated with the faithful and root for them to uncover a traitor had their wish firmly Richard E Grant-ed on Thursday, as the actor was banished in a landslide vote.His questionable strategy of revealing he was a traitor to the other celebrities in the bar led to the first time in the UK version of the show that a traitor has been identified at the opening round table."Thank you for giving me an almost bingo full-house of votes," Grant told his fellow players. "I have always wanted to be a traitor, and sometimes in life your dreams do come true."There was jubilation from the other celebrities as Grant confirmed his identity, waving his hands in the air. Ross Kemp was so happy it came out as borderline anger, with a vein-popping "get in there!"Other players seemed genuinely shocked. "This is me with men all the time," joked comedian Joanne McNally, who hadn't voted for Grant. "I completely believed him!"But although the faithful had successfully found a traitor, and even managed to spell his name correctly on their slates, the first round table saw some other players behave in ways that immediately aroused suspicion.Image caption, Myha'la winked at Richard E Grant before voting for him - which was picked up by some other playersImage caption, Ross Kemp, meanwhile, was a scary level of delighted to have rumbled GrantJulie Hesmondhalgh noticed Myha'la ostentatiously winking at Grant before she voted for him, which later prompted the former Coronation Street actress to make one of the most impassioned - but mistaken - speeches of the night."It was traitor-on-traitor," she declared (it wasn't). "I don't know if anybody else saw it," (we did). "I am so excited because I truly believe we can get two in a row," (don't count on it).Where is the Traitors castle, and can you visit it?Traitors commit first murder as Grant tries to save his skinCelebrity Traitors cast: Who are this year's 'big dogs' and dark horses?The remaining traitors, Maya Jama and James Acaster, met in the turret later with the choice of murdering previously shortlisted players Jerry Hall and Hannah Fry, or seducing a third traitor to replace Grant.The pair ultimately decided to recruit mathematician Fry, who had the most wonderful and meme-able reaction when she found out that, not only was she not being murdered, she was being seduced.Accepting the offer, Fry joined Jama and Acaster in the turret, exclaiming as she learned their identities: "I had both of you down as faithful!"The new trio discussed how they would approach breakfast the next morning, before Acaster delivered the line of the episode."It's changing a lot, this Traitors," he observed of the fluid line-up. "It's like the Sugababes."Image caption, "I managed to checkmate myself," said Grant, "which as far as I'm aware, has never been done"Image caption, Mathematician Hannah Fry was shocked to find she was being recruited instead of murderedThe next morning, there were shocked faces when the players realised everybody had made it to breakfast unscathed, with the celebrities concluding that one player must have been recruited."It was fascinating seeing Jerry and Hannah come back," said Miranda Hart. "Hannah seemed different, as if something new has happened to her." Oh yes? "I definitely clocked a nervousness in her, which is very interesting."We could have a first-rate traitor hunter on our hands here. But would any of Hart's fellow players feel the same way? "Poor Hannah," said McNally, "she's been recruited." Uh-oh.As the theories continued to float around across various sub-meetings, with Hesmondhalgh, Bella Ramsey and several others setting their sights on Myha'la, the celebrities headed out to the next mission. Presenter Claudia Winkleman explained the latest task would see them use a battering ram to break down the doors of four crypts, where they could find money to add to the prize pot - and also potentially bag some shields.James Blunt immediately took control, assigning players various roles. "He was full army officer," Hart observed. "I found it mildly erotic.""I don't think I've ever used a battering ram," Joe Lycett reflected. "I would use a battering ram to get into [Wicked star] Jonathan Bailey's house, but that's it."Image caption, Miranda Hart joked that she found James Blunt's command of the latest task "mildly erotic"Myha'la and Fry entered one crypt, found a shield and debated who should keep it. They agreed on Myha'la, partly because she had grabbed it first, although she sweetly suggested that the pair could keep it secret from the other players to protect both of them.Jama and Sharon Rooney, meanwhile, scored two further shields, but the players then found that some shields would have to be given up anyway in order to unlock the final chest of prize money.Rooney and Myha'la surrendered theirs, but traitor Jama quietly held on to hers. The other players didn't know she had one, and the TV presenter asked Rooney to keep it secret. That decision could come back to bite her in later episodes.In the cars on the way back, the players continued to debate various hunches, with one particularly awkward journey where Myha'la and Hesmondhalgh admitted they were suspicious of each other."I feel like you've been a little bit vague," said Hesmondhalgh. "That's only because I've thought it's been you from day one," Myha'la replied.We've certainly come a long way from the pair's first exchange just two episodes ago. "It's lovely to meet you Myha'la, I'm such a big fan!" - "Oh my God, thank you!"Back in the castle, Rob Beckett had adopted a new policy. "When someone comes up to talk to me, I just agree with them, whatever they say," he laughed in the castle's diary room.Image caption, James Acaster joked that he wanted to murder James Blunt to avoid confusion over them sharing a nameAs the players gathered for the second banishment of the episode, discussion inevitably turned to prime suspect Myha'la."I've heard my name a whole bunch today," she acknowledged, as the others struggled to square her behaviour during the mission.The actress became visibly emotional as she recounted the events of the crypt and attempted to justify grabbing the shield before offering it to Fry. "I was going to give it to her," Myha'la said tearfully. "I was worried about my protection, but I thought maybe [Fry] had more heat."Sensing that the tide was turning against Myha'la, Fry stuck the knife in. "Why would you scrabble for the shield, and then be keen to give it away?" she asked.Watch on iPlayer with new episodes every Thursday and Friday The latest banished and murdered celebs have their say in UncloakedDespite a sprinkling of votes for other players, Myha'la became the second casualty of the episode. "I have loved getting to know you all," she said as she confirmed her faithful status to the other players. Hart became even more suspicious of Fry, however, after realising the mathematician had orchestrated events to make Myha'la's behaviour at the crypt look less innocent. "Miss Marple is so on," Hart said with a smile.Later, the traitors met in the turret and debated who their next victim should be, settling on a shortlist of Blunt, Ramsey and Sebastian Croft.Acaster had a characteristically unique reason for suggesting James Blunt. "It would make my life easier," he said, "because every time someone says 'James', I'm turning around, and half the time, it's for him."Celebrity Traitors continues on Friday at 20:00 BST on BBC One and iPlayer.Get in touchHave you played a version of the Traitors or another social deduction game at home or socially? Share your experience.

schema.headline: Celebrity Traitors episode three: Emotions run high as two players banished

title: Hoads Wood illegal waste "supersite" finally cleared at £15m cost
description: £15m spent cleaning illegal waste supersite in ancient woodlandImage source, Getty Images/BBC/Rachel PriceImage caption, The Hoads Wood site before an
body: £15m spent cleaning illegal waste supersite in ancient woodlandImage source, Getty Images/BBC/Rachel PriceImage caption, The Hoads Wood site before and after it was cleared of nearly 40,000 tonnes of wasteByJenny KumahRural affairs correspondent and Malcolm PriorRural affairs producerThe clearance of a notorious illegal waste "supersite" in Kent has been completed after 15 months at a cost of £15m to the taxpayer. The dump at Hoads Wood, near Ashford, which is on a Site of Special Scientific Interest (SSSI) known for rare plants and wildlife, was targeted by criminals who dumped nearly 40,000 tonnes of waste over six months in 2023. It was the first supersite in England to have central government money spent on its clear-up, with work at two other sites bringing the total taxpayer's bill to £26m.The government said the completion of works on Friday showed "just how serious" it was about tackling waste crime and restoring affected countryside.Image source, PA MediaImage caption, It took 2,500 lorry loads to clear the waste which had been dumped by criminal gangsThe Environment Agency-led clean-up operation began in June 2025 and has seen 2,500 lorry loads of waste removed from the woods by specialist contractors to a landfill site in Essex.The countryside charity CPRE Kent, residents and Kent Wildlife Trust joined forces in 2024 to campaign for the clearance of the waste, which was piled up to 15ft (4.6m) in places.They welcomed the work's completion but some are concerned the criminal gangs may return to dump waste.One of the organisers of the 'Rescue Hoads Wood' campaign said the cleared site would now be "catnip" to both organised gangs and opportunist fly-tippers.He told the BBC: "Our biggest fear now is people are going to be able to access this site and start dumping on it again and unless the authorities are quick it will happen again."The Environment Agency (EA) said it was extending the current restriction order in place that prohibits access and had dug ditches to make the site inaccessible to waste trucks.Matthew Higginson, the EA's area environmental manager, said the regulator, police and local authorities had a joint "trigger plan" in place."That will bring all law enforcement partners to work together closely and much more quickly to stop anything like this happening in the future," he said. Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, The rubbish was illegally dumped in an ancient bluebell woodlandMeanwhile, there remain conservation concerns over the future of the countryside site.Ian Rickards, area manager for Kent Wildlife Trust, said it would take decades for ancient woodland species to return.But he added: "It won't recover as it was but there are benefits to this. You've now got open space within the woodland. You've got wet bodies. You've got ponds. You've got these piles of dead wood as well. "All of this will start creating, collecting and attracting wildlife back into here so it'll be fascinating to see how the site recovers."Image source, Jenny Kumah/BBCImage caption, Ian Rickards, from Kent Wildlife Trust, is hopeful new flora and fauna will eventually appear in the woodsThe Hoads Wood illegal waste site is one of hundreds across England that include a number of so-called "supersites" - those that contain more than 20,000 tonnes of rubbish - that were exposed by the BBC earlier this year.As well as the £15m spent on clearing Hoads Wood, another £6m has been spent on the clearance of an illegal supersite in Kidlington, Oxfordshire, and a further £4.8m of taxpayers' money has been allocated to the clear-up of a third site near Wigan.Speed of authorities criticisedIn August, the government launched a national action plan to tackle waste crime, which it estimates costs the country more than £1bn every year.But Hoads Wood campaigners have criticised the authorities for not acting quickly enough when the illegal tipping was first reported at the Kent site.At the height of the activity in the summer of 2023, locals said there were as many as 20 to 30 trucks per day dumping waste at the ancient bluebell woodland.The EA's Matthew Higginson said the agency did respond quickly to reports of the dumping but had to spend time investigating "to make sure we had a robust case to take to court in order to get a restriction order which closed the site".Investigations into who was behind the dumping are ongoing, with three arrests made in February 2025.Environment secretary Dame Angela Eagle said: "This government is taking action on the illegal waste sites that have blighted communities."Handing this ancient woodland back to local people, alongside our nationwide clean-up of waste sites, shows just how serious we are about restoring the places people love."Get in touchIs there a new illegal waste dump in your area? Tell us.

schema.headline: Hoads Wood illegal waste "supersite" finally cleared at £15m cost

title: Manchester City charges: Enzo Maresca says 'titles absolutely not tainted'
description: Manchester City manager Enzo Maresca says the club's titles are "absolutely not" tainted after they were found guilty of the majority of the 115 charg
body: Manchester City manager Enzo Maresca says the club's titles are "absolutely not" tainted after they were found guilty of the majority of the 115 charges brought against them by the Premier League.Maresca reiterated his faith in the club's owners and belief that they will win their appeal against the verdict during a news conference on Friday dominated by questions on the matter.The Italian, notably relaxed as he offered his responses, rejected the suggestion City's titles have been tainted by the ruling, as he knows "exactly the effort that the club put in to achieve" them.An independent commission found Manchester City guilty of all charges relating to breaches of the Premier League's financial regulations between the 2009-10 and 2017-18 seasons.The club have appealed against the verdict and claimed in a statement the commission's ruling contained "clear material errors, of law, principle and fact and is unsafe".Preparing to play their first match since that verdict was announced, away to rivals Liverpool on Sunday, Maresca said in an in-house interview on Thursday the "feeling is fantastic" among his players and they are not affected by "the noise" surrounding the club.He added on Friday: "The reason I joined this club is that I completely trust, 100%, the owner, the CEO, the sporting director, all the organisation. So I don't have doubt about that."I spoke with the club for sure. We all trust, and probably the right moment to speak about that is when we are going to win this appeal."He added: "For me, the players - we can control just the pitch side, the football side. So we are focused on that. This is what we can do and what we can control."Appointed as Pep Guardiola's successor in June, Maresca is in his third spell at the club following time spent with the academy and as Guardiola's assistant coach - including during the Treble-winning 2022-23 campaign.The 46-year-old has won each of his first five Premier League games in charge of City, and could become the fourth manager to win his first six of a spell in charge of a club in the competition at Liverpool on Sunday.The announcement of the verdict reached by an independent panel, which found City guilty of 'sham' contracts and misleading accounts as part of a scheme to disguise secret funding of more than £830m, means Maresca's side will expect to receive an even more hostile reception than usual at Anfield.Asked if he had any concerns over the atmosphere during the match, Maresca said: "It will be a tough game, for sure. We need to be ready, the focus needs to be about the game, but we know the environment at Anfield. "It probably will be worse because of the situation but, again, it will be our duty to do our best and try to win the game."The reason I decide to become manager is for this type of game."Maresca thanked one journalist who asked a question not related to the verdict, confirming talisman Erling Haaland is "ready" to play against Liverpool after recovering from his efforts for Norway during the international break in Marbella.

schema.headline: Manchester City charges: Enzo Maresca says 'titles absolutely not tainted'

title: Singapore Grand Prix: George Russell fastest from Charles Leclerc in only practice session
description: Mercedes driver George Russell led Ferrari's Charles Leclerc in practice at the Singapore Grand Prix.A late lap from Leclerc, who was 0.198 seconds of
body: Mercedes driver George Russell led Ferrari's Charles Leclerc in practice at the Singapore Grand Prix.A late lap from Leclerc, who was 0.198 seconds off Russell's pace, split up what had been an all-British top three.McLaren's Lando Norris was third fastest, 0.273secs behind Russell, and Ferrari's Lewis Hamilton fourth, 0.499secs off the pace.The top five, concluded by McLaren's Oscar Piastri, were all on the soft-compound tyres, while Red Bull's Max Verstappen was the fastest driver using medium tyres in sixth place.The four-time champion was 0.732secs off the pace and 0.519secs quicker than Mercedes' Kimi Antonelli behind him in seventh, also on the medium tyres.It was the only practice session of the weekend with sprint qualifying taking place at 13:30 BST.The split between tyre compounds made it hard to form any conclusions about relative pace.Russell will start Sunday's race from the back as a result of a penalty for using too many engine parts, following his engine failure while running third in the closing stages of the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia.He and Antonelli are also running different specifications of car, Russell reverting to a previous spec and the Italian the new aerodynamic package introduced in Malaysia.This is so Mercedes can get a better read of whether the upgrade package is working after struggling for pace in Malaysia when they expected to make a step forward.Verstappen took his and Red Bull's first win of the year at Sepang, and looked quick at times in the session before tyre strategies diverged.His team-mate Isack Hadjar, also on the medium, was eighth fastest, with Alpine's Pierre Gasly and Racing Bulls' Liam Lawson completing the top 10.Aston Martin's Fernando Alonso was in the top 10 for a time, but dropped back in the closing stages of the session to end up 14th.The racing action is taking place amid air-quality warnings in Singapore as a result of haze from wildfires in Indonesia, primarily caused by illegal slash-and-burn practices used by farmers and companies as a cheap method to clear vegetation.This is leading to record levels of air pollution in the city state and citizens are advised to limit outdoor activities.

schema.headline: Singapore Grand Prix: George Russell fastest from Charles Leclerc in only practice session
